label: Figure O.1 — How data can support development: A theory of change
summary: A theory-of-change diagram links data production and collection, data analytics and processing across three groups, and development. Reuse connects the groups; the diagram contrasts potential positive impacts (green) with negative impacts (red).
details: The diagram is arranged left to right. At left is a circle labeled “Data production and collection.” In the central shaded column, headed “Data analytics and processing,” three boxes are stacked: “Individuals / Civil society / Academia,” “Government / International organizations,” and “Private sector.” Two-way vertical arrows labeled “Reuse” connect the top and middle boxes and the middle and bottom boxes. Dotted side routes with arrowheads also connect the top and bottom groups. Gray arrows link data production and collection with the central groups: the upper route is labeled “Greater transparency,” the horizontal two-way link “More data on individuals,” and the lower route “Production process in firms.” Routes from the central groups lead to the right-hand circle labeled “Development.” The top route is labeled in green “Greater accountability” and in red “Criminal activity, dark net”; the middle route in green “Better policy making and service delivery” and in red “Political surveillance”; the bottom route in green “Increased business opportunities” and in red “Market concentration / Widening inequality / Discrimination.” Source: WDR 2021 team. Note: “Positive impacts are shown in green; negative impacts are shown in red.”
limitations: Arrow routes are visible, but some line intersections and arrowheads are small; no numerical data are shown. The upper and lower routes include bends, so their precise connections are interpreted from the visible arrowheads and labels.

label: Map O.1
summary: Weekly maps of cellphone-record mobility flows across administrative districts in The Gambia during COVID-19 lockdowns, March–May 2020.
details: The figure contains 11 small maps of The Gambia, labeled Week 3 through Week 13: Week 3, March 15–21; Week 4, March 22–28; Week 5, March 29–April 4; Week 6, April 5–11; Week 7, April 12–18; Week 8, April 19–25; Week 9, April 26–May 2; Week 10, May 3–9; Week 11, May 10–16; Week 12, May 17–23; and Week 13, May 24–30. Districts are shaded by percentage change in population flows, with a blue-to-green scale labeled −60, −40, −20, −16, −12, −8, −4, 0, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 40, and 60+. Blue indicates outflow of people; green indicates inflow. Map labels include Banjul, Brikama, Kanifing, Kerewan, Mansa Konko, Georgetown, Basse, and Santa Su. Legend symbols identify national capital and district capitals; line styles identify international and district boundaries. Source: Knippenberg and Meyer 2020; data link printed as http://bit.do/WDR2021-Map-O_1. Note states that a nationwide lockdown was imposed on March 22, 2020, and data were gathered using call detail records.
limitations: Small district-level labels and individual color assignments are difficult to read at this resolution; no specific district values are stated.

label: Figure O.2 — A social contract for data founded on value, trust, and equity
summary: Three interlocking hexagons present value, trust, and equity as foundations of a social contract for data.
details: The diagram has three large colored hexagons arranged around a central orange triangular overlap labeled “THE SOCIAL CONTRACT.” The upper blue hexagon is labeled “VALUE” and states: “The full value of data materializes when systems enable the use and reuse of data for different purposes.” The lower-left green hexagon is labeled “TRUST” and states: “A trust environment is created when the rights and interests that all stakeholders have in data are safeguarded.” The lower-right purple hexagon is labeled “EQUITY” and states: “All share equitably in the benefits of data when investments and regulations create a level playing field.” Source printed below: “WDR 2021 team.”
limitations: No directional arrows or quantitative values are shown.

label: Map O.2 — Highly refined data pinpointed areas of Nigeria that needed better sanitation
summary: Choropleth map of Nigeria showing the share of the population with inadequate access to improved sanitation, by geographic area; Abuja is marked as the national capital.
details: Nigeria is filled with area-level colors and outlined internal state boundaries; international boundaries are also identified in the legend. The legend categories for “% of population with inadequate access to improved sanitation” are 0–19.9, 20–39.9, 40–59.9, 60–79.9, and 80–100. Colors progress from dark teal through green and pale yellow to orange-red. A star marks Abuja as the national capital. Source printed below map: World Bank 2017; data link shown as http://bit.do/WDR2021-Map-O_2. Map imprint: IBRD NIR45641 | MARCH 2021. Note states that geographic hotspots are shown from least severe to most severe in terms of the percentage of the population in the area that meets an international benchmark for sanitation; the note’s wording appears inconsistent with the legend’s “inadequate access” measure.
limitations: No individual area values are printed on the map; only the five legend ranges are readable. The note uses wording about the percentage meeting a benchmark, while the legend describes inadequate access.

label: Map O.3 — Combining satellite imagery with household survey data increases the resolution of the poverty map of Tanzania
summary: Two 2018 Tanzania poverty-incidence maps compare a Household Budget Survey map for 20 regions with a finer map combining that survey data and satellite imagery for 169 districts.
details: The figure has two side-by-side panels. (a) “Poverty map using the Household Budget Survey (20 regions)” shows regional boundaries and names. Its legend is “Poverty incidence, 2018 (% of population)”: 36–45, 32–35, 26–31, 22–25, 8–21, and No data. It also marks the national capital, international boundaries, and province boundaries. (b) “Poverty map combining the data in panel a with satellite imagery (169 districts)” shows finer district boundaries. Its legend uses the same measure and year, with classes 38–67, 31–37, 24–30, 17–23, 4–16, and No data; it also marks the national capital, international boundaries, and district boundaries. Both maps depict Tanzania, including mainland and Zanzibar; Dodoma is marked as the national capital. Source: World Bank 2019; data link printed as http://bit.do/WDR2021-Map-O_3. Map identifier printed near the lower right: IBRD TAN45642 | MARCH 2021.
limitations: The maps encode ranges by color; individual locations do not have printed numeric incidence values. Some small district shapes and labels are difficult to distinguish at this page scale. The panels use different poverty-class intervals, so the color categories are not identical.

label: Figure O.3
summary: Matrix of four data-governance layers, showing policy areas at national and international levels.
details:
Title: “Data governance layers at the national and international levels.” Three columns: governance layer; National; International. Rows and contents:
• Infrastructure policies — National: Universal coverage of broadband networks; domestic infrastructure to exchange, store, and process data. International: Global technical standards for compatibility of hardware and software; regional collaboration on data infrastructure to achieve scale.
• Laws and regulations — National: Safeguards to secure and protect data from the threat of misuse; enablers to facilitate data sharing among different stakeholders. International: Cybersecurity conventions for collaboration on tackling cybercrime; interoperability standards to facilitate data exchanges across borders.
• Economic policies — National: Antitrust for data platform businesses; trade in data-enabled services; taxation of data platform businesses. International: International tax treaties to allocate taxation rights across countries; global trade agreements on cross-border trade in data-enabled services.
• Institutions — National: Government entities to oversee, regulate, and secure data; other stakeholders to set standards and increase data access and reuse. International: International organizations to support collaboration on data governance and promote standardization; cooperation on cross-border regulatory spillovers and enforcement issues.
Source: WDR 2021 team.
limitations: No quantitative values or directional links are shown; the visual organizes examples by layer and governance level.

label: Map O.4 — Data infrastructure is not yet widespread across all parts of the world
summary: World map showing locations of colocation data centers, internet exchange points, submarine cable landing stations, and submarine cables.
details: The map covers the world, with land shaded light gray and infrastructure marked by a legend: red dots = colocation data centers; blue dots = internet exchange points (IXPs); open black circles = submarine cable landing stations; green lines = submarine cables. Infrastructure markers and cable routes are dense across North America, Europe, and parts of East and Southeast Asia, with substantial cable networks connecting continents and island regions. Markers and routes are more sparsely distributed across much of Africa, Central Asia, and parts of South America. Sources listed beneath the map: PeeringDB; PCH Packet Clearing House (IXP locations, accessed December 14, 2020); and TeleGeography submarine cables. Data URL: http://bit.do/WDR2021-Map-O_4. Map imprint: IBRD WLD45643 | MARCH 2021.
limitations: This is a schematic global map; individual symbols and cable routes overlap densely in some regions, so exact counts and precise locations cannot be reliably read from the image.

label: Figure O.4
summary: Radar chart comparing the percentage of good-practice data governance laws and regulatory measures across four country income groups and seven regulatory areas.
details: Seven-axis radar chart with a 0–90 scale in increments of 10. Axes clockwise from top: E-commerce framework; Enabling access to public intent data; Enabling access to private intent data; Cybersecurity; Personal data protection; Nonpersonal data protection; Cross-border data flows. Series: High-income (blue), Upper-middle-income (green), Lower-middle-income (orange), Low-income (purple). Approximate plotted values by axis, read from the grid: High-income 85, 65, 40, 65, 55, 45, 40; Upper-middle-income 70, 60, 35, 45, 40, 40, 25; Lower-middle-income 65, 45, 25, 40, 40, 35, 20; Low-income 45, 25, 15, 30, 30, 40, 15. The chart compares coverage across income groups; high-income is generally highest, while values are comparatively low for enabling access to private intent data and cross-border data flows. Source: WDR 2021 team, based on the Global Data Regulation Survey conducted exclusively for the Report. Note: Figure depicts the percentage of good-practice laws and regulatory measures in place for countries covered by the survey in each income group.
limitations: Values are approximate visual readings from the radar chart; exact data values are not printed. The grid scale and overlapping series make some points difficult to distinguish precisely.

label: Figure O.5
summary: Global trade in data-driven services and digital data flows, 1990–2018; data-driven services rise substantially and account for about half of services trade by 2018, while IP traffic grows sharply.
details: Title: “Since 1990, the global trade in data-driven services has grown exponentially and now constitutes half of trade in services.” The chart combines stacked areas for services trade (left axis, US$ billions, current; 0–6,000) and vertical bars for IP traffic (right axis, PB per month; 0–100,000). The horizontal axis shows each year from 1990 through 2018. Stacked-area legend: computer, communications, and other services; travel services; transport services; other (unclassified). Bar series: IP traffic (right axis). In-chart labels distinguish “Data-driven services” from “Traditional services” and identify “Global digital data flows.” Overall, services trade grows from under US$1,000 billion in 1990 to nearly US$6,000 billion in 2018; IP traffic rises from near zero to close to 100,000 PB per month by 2018. Source: WDR 2021 team calculations, based on World Bank, WITS database. Note: IP = Internet Protocol; PB = petabytes.
limitations: The chart does not print numeric data labels for individual years or series, so precise annual values and exact component amounts cannot be read reliably. The source note includes a data URL.

label: Figure O.6 — What happens in an integrated national data system?
summary: Diagram of an integrated national data system, showing what happens to data, who participates, the system’s pillars, and the foundation sustaining it.
details: Four stacked, outlined sections. “Data are”: produced; protected; open; quality controlled; used and reused. “By”: government entities; civil society and individuals; academic institutions; the private sector; international organizations. “Built on the pillars of”: infrastructure policies; laws and regulations; economic policies; institutions. “Sustained by the foundation of”: human capital; trust; funding; incentives; data demand. Source: WDR 2021 team.
limitations: The diagram groups items into four sections but does not show directional arrows or specify relationships among items within each section.

label: Figure 1.1
summary: World population enumerated in censuses rose from 11% in 1850 to 90% in 2010, alongside growth in total world population.
details: Title: “The share of people counted in a census grew from about 1 in 10 in 1850 to 9 in 10 today.” Horizontal axis: decades 1850–2010. Vertical axis: World population (billions), 0–8. The shaded area represents world population, increasing from about 1.2 billion in 1850 to about 7.7 billion in 2010; green bars show the percentage enumerated each decade. Percentages printed above/in bars: 1850 11%, 1860 14%, 1870 17%, 1880 21%, 1890 38%, 1900 51%, 1910 44%, 1920 46%, 1930 58%, 1940 58%, 1950 82%, 1960 94%, 1970 71%, 1980 92%, 1990 92%, 2000 88%, 2010 90%. Source: Whitby 2020; data link printed as http://bit.do/WDR2021-Fig-1_1. Note: bars indicate the share enumerated each decade; shaded area indicates world population. Values for population are read approximately from the plotted area, not individually labeled.
limitations: Population-area values are not labeled numerically at each decade; approximate readings only. The chart’s “today” wording refers to its latest plotted year, 2010.

label: Map 1.1
summary: John Snow’s map of London’s 1854 cholera epidemic, illustrating the locations of cholera deaths.
details: A black-and-white historical street map of part of London, with street and place labels and solid black rectangles of varying sizes marking cholera deaths. The map is captioned: “John Snow’s innovative mapping of the cholera epidemic in London in 1854 revolutionized tracing of the disease.” Source: Ball 2009; map segment reproduced from John Snow, On the Mode of Communication of Cholera, 2nd ed. (London: John Churchill, 1855).
limitations: Individual map labels and the exact number or locations of death markers are not reliably legible at this resolution. The note identifies the black rectangles as deaths from cholera.

label: Table 1.1 — Examples of data types based on original intent and collection methods
summary: Examples classified by data collection method (traditional or new) and original intent (public or private).
details: Columns: Data collection methods and tools | Public intent data | Private intent data. Traditional: Public—Census, national accounts, household surveys, enterprise surveys, labor force surveys, surveys of personal finance, administrative records. Private—Any survey conducted by private entities, including public opinion surveys deployed by private entities; administrative data from company financial accounts. New: Public—Location data from satellite imaging, digital identification, facial recognition from public cameras, public procurement data from e-government platforms. Private—Just-in-time digital data on individual behavior/choices from digital platforms in the private sector. Source printed below table: WDR 2021 team.
limitations: No numeric values or units; the table presents examples. Bounding box includes the source line immediately below the table.

label: Figure 1.2 — The data life cycle
summary: Circular data life-cycle diagram: Create/receive, Process, Store, Transfer/share, Analyze and use, Archive and preserve, and Destroy, with Reuse at the center.
details: Outer cycle stages, in clockwise order: Create/receive (top), Process (upper right), Store (lower right), Transfer/share (bottom), Analyze and use (lower left), Archive and preserve (upper left). Broad curved arrows connect the main stages around the loop. Reuse is central, connected by lines to the surrounding stages, indicating reuse across the cycle. A separate arrow points from Archive and preserve toward Destroy. Source printed below: “Source: WDR 2021 team.”
limitations: Diagram shows relationships but no numerical data. Direction of the full outer cycle is indicated by arrows; small connector lines between Reuse and stages do not show additional directional arrows.

label: Figure 1.3 — Three pathways along which data can foster development
summary: Diagram showing data production and collection feeding data analytics and processing, with reuse by individuals/civil society/academia, government/international organizations, and the private sector; these pathways can foster development through positive outcomes but also carry negative impacts.
details: The diagram places “Data production and collection” at left, a central vertical “Data analytics and processing” pathway, and “Development” at right. The central pathway contains three boxes, from top to bottom: “Individuals / Civil society / Academia,” “Government / International organizations,” and “Private sector.” Dotted vertical connections between the boxes are labeled “Reuse” and show arrows in both directions; dotted side connections also link the analytics/processing area with the upper and lower boxes. The left-to-center inputs are labeled “Greater transparency” (upper route), “More data on individuals” (middle route), and “Production process in firms” (lower route). Positive impacts are printed in green and negative impacts in red: upper route, “Greater accountability” and “Criminal activity, dark net”; government route, “Better policy making and service delivery” and “Political surveillance”; private-sector route, “Increased business opportunities” and “Market concentration / Widening inequality / Discrimination.” Arrows connect the labeled routes and outcomes toward development; the upper and lower routes also show arrows returning toward data production and collection. Source: WDR 2021 team. Note: Positive impacts are shown in green; negative impacts are shown in red.
limitations: Some dotted side arrows are faint; their precise direction is less clear than the solid route arrows. No numerical values are shown.

label: Figure B1.4.1 — Use of repurposed data to study COVID-19: Published articles, by type of private intent data used
summary: Stacked area chart of articles using different types of private-intent data to study COVID-19, from February to September 2020. The cumulative total rises sharply from near zero in February to just over 1,000 by September; social media is the largest category throughout the later period.
details: The horizontal axis is time in 2020, with labels February, April, July, and September. The vertical axis is “Number of articles,” marked 0, 250, 500, 750, and 1,000. The stacked categories, from bottom to top in the legend, are Social media, Twitter, Big data, Google Trends, Facebook, Cellphone, and Call detail records. The plotted total is near zero early in the period, rises notably after April, and reaches slightly above the 1,000 gridline by September. Social media forms the largest area at the end (roughly 530 articles by visual estimation); Twitter is the next largest (roughly 200), with smaller areas for Big data and Google Trends, and comparatively small Facebook, Cellphone, and Call detail records areas. These are visual estimates, not labeled data values. The note says the figure counts articles published in scientific, medical, and technical journals from February to September 2020, and that the sum across categories is higher because some articles appear in more than one category. Source: WDR 2021 team, based on CORD-19 data from the Semantic Scholar team, Ai2.
limitations: Exact category values are not printed on the chart and should not be inferred from the stacked areas. The cumulative sum across categories can include the same article more than once.

label: Map B1.4.1 — Use of repurposed data to study COVID-19: Published articles, by country
summary: World choropleth showing country-level counts of published COVID-19 research articles, adjusted by COVID-19 death incidence rate, February–September 2020.
details: The map shades countries using a yellow-to-green/teal-to-dark-purple scale. The legend is titled “Number of articles” and shows reference values 7.5, 10.0, 12.5, and 15.0; gray denotes “No data.” Country shading varies widely: China is among the darkest purple areas, while many countries are shown in intermediate green/teal shades and some in yellow. The note states that the map covers articles published in scientific, medical, and technical journals from February to September 2020, and that article counts are divided by the COVID-19 death incidence rate. Source: WDR 2021 team, based on CORD-19 data from the Semantic Scholar team, Ai2. Exact country-level values are not printed on the map; colors indicate the mapped scale.
limitations: The legend provides only selected reference values, not numeric break boundaries for every color. Individual country values cannot be read exactly from the map.

label: Figure 1.4 — Data governance layers at the national and international levels
summary: Four data-governance layers compare policy priorities at national and international levels: infrastructure policies, laws and regulations, economic policies, and institutions.
details:
The diagram has four horizontal rows. Each row pairs an illustrated layer label at left with National and International columns.

• Infrastructure policies — National: “Universal coverage of broadband networks”; “Domestic infrastructure to exchange, store, and process data.” International: “Global technical standards for compatibility of hardware and software”; “Regional collaboration on data infrastructure to achieve scale.”
• Laws and regulations — National: “Safeguards to secure and protect data from the threat of misuse”; “Enablers to facilitate data sharing among different stakeholders.” International: “Cybersecurity conventions for collaboration on tackling cybercrime”; “Interoperability standards to facilitate data exchanges across borders.”
• Economic policies — National: “Antitrust for data platform businesses”; “Trade in data-enabled services”; “Taxation of data platform businesses.” International: “International tax treaties to allocate taxation rights across countries”; “Global trade agreements on cross-border trade in data-enabled services.”
• Institutions — National: “Government entities to oversee, regulate, and secure data”; “Other stakeholders to set standards and increase data access and reuse.” International: “International organizations to support collaboration on data governance and promote standardization”; “Cooperation on cross-border regulatory spillovers and enforcement issues.”
Source: WDR 2021 team.
limitations: The figure is legible. The native text contains a likely OCR error (“dierent”); the image reads “different.”

label: Figure 1.5
summary: Diagram of data flowing safely among five stakeholder groups in an integrated national data system, with a connected pathway of five data attributes.
details: The figure is titled “Data flow safely across all stakeholders in an integrated national data system.” Five blue-outlined circular nodes—Academic institutions, Government entities, International organizations, Private sector, and Civil society and individuals—surround a central area labeled “Data.” Multiple intersecting green pathways with directional arrowheads connect the stakeholder nodes and pass around and through the central data area, depicting flows among stakeholders. Below, a “Data attributes” sequence shows five labeled icons connected left to right: Produced → Protected → Open → Quality controlled → Used and reused. Source: WDR 2021 team.
limitations: The many crossing pathways and arrowheads make individual routes between specific stakeholder pairs ambiguous; the figure does not label particular transactions or assign data attributes to individual routes.

label: Figure S1.1.1 — A citizen-led method to ascertain who has authority in household decision-making in rural Indian villages
summary: A screenshot-style matrix compares household decision-making authority across four decisions and two village groups. Larger family-member faces indicate greater authority; greener backgrounds indicate greater authority for women.
details: The visual has four decision rows and two comparison columns, with a question and illustrative icon at left. Row questions: (1) whether the respondent’s opinion is accepted regarding a child’s education and marriage; (2) who makes decisions regarding clothing; (3) who makes decisions regarding the number of children; and (4) who decides when to visit the respondent’s parents’ house. Each row shows family-member faces in both comparison columns, with varying relative face sizes and background shades. The column header text appears to read “H1 Agam…” and “H9 Manalath…”; the full names are not reliably legible. No numeric values or scale are shown. The printed note says face size represents relative authority over a decision and that backgrounds shade from dark gray toward dark green when women have more authority.
limitations: The screenshot is small and some village names, labels, and facial details are indistinct. The visual gives qualitative comparisons only; no exact measurements or legend scale are visible.

label: Figure S1.2.1
summary: Grouped horizontal bars compare the composition of DSSI-eligible countries’ bilateral debt by creditor in 2013 and 2019; China’s share rose markedly while the share of other G-20 bilateral creditors fell.
details: Title: “In six years, the composition of debt has shifted dramatically.” Subtitle: “DSSI-eligible countries’ bilateral debt: Composition of creditors, 2013 and 2019.” Horizontal axis: “% of bilateral debt,” from 0 to 60, with ticks at 0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, and 60. Legend: blue = 2013; green = 2019. Categories and approximate bar endpoints (%): China, 38 (2013) and 57 (2019); Other G-20 bilateral creditors, 29 and 18; Japan, 13 and 13; India, 4 and 4; Other bilateral creditors, 15 and 9. Source: World Bank, Debt Data (dashboard); source note also provides a data link. Note refers readers to the World Bank’s External Debt Reporting System information and expands DSSI as Debt Service Suspension Initiative.
limitations: Bar values are not printed numerically; values above are approximate readings from the axis and bar endpoints. The 2019 China bar ends just below 60, approximately 57.

label: Box 2.1 — Six types of public intent data
summary: A two-column illustrated overview of six public-intent data types, with descriptions and examples; notes that the types can overlap and be interoperable.
details: The box presents six types with icons: Administrative data (registration and record-keeping, including birth, marriage, death, identification, population, health, education, tax, trade-flow, and government project/program/service data); Censuses (systematic enumeration of a population of interest, including population and housing censuses); Sample surveys (representative samples used for more frequent detailed information across household, farm, enterprise, labor-force, and demographic/health domains); Citizen-generated data (individual-produced data that can fill gaps or support monitoring and accountability; examples: HarassMap and ForestWatchers); Machine-generated data (automatically produced by sensors, applications, or computer processes; example: air-pollution sensors and the Internet of Things); and Geospatial data (information layers associated with geographic location; examples include Landsat and Copernicus satellite imagery, weather, and cadastral data). A concluding note says the types are neither exhaustive nor mutually exclusive: sources can be georeferenced, and some administrative and geospatial data can be machine-generated. Interoperability can use common numeric identifiers, geospatial coordinates, time stamps, and classification standards. Three footnotes discuss social-media surveys, cite Meijer and Potjer (2018), and refer readers to chapter 4.
limitations: The box is text-led and has no quantitative values. The six icons are illustrative; no additional legend is shown.

label: Figure 2.1 — Certain data features can maximize the value of public intent data
summary: Four adjacent columns group data features under coverage, quality, ease of use, and safety of use.
details: From left to right: “Ensuring the data have adequate coverage” lists Completeness, Timeliness, Frequency; “Ensuring the data are of high quality” lists Granularity, Accuracy, Comparability; “Ensuring the data are easy to use” lists Accessibility, Understandability, Interoperability; “Ensuring the data are safe to use” lists Impartiality, Confidentiality, Appropriateness. Source: WDR 2021 team, drawing on Jolliffe et al. (forthcoming).
limitations: The graphic is a categorical grouping, with no axes, numerical scale, or indicated ranking.

label: Figure 2.2
summary: Kenya hand-pump repair times fell with mobile-enabled sensor data: median repair time decreased from 6 to 1 day, and mean repair time from 27 to 2.6 days.
details: Horizontal bar chart titled “Improving access to water: Using real-time sensor data to reduce repair time for broken hand pumps in Kenya.” The x-axis is “Number of days,” from 0 to 30. Categories are Median repair time and Mean repair time. Legend: blue = With mobile-enabled data; green = Baseline. Median: 1 day with mobile-enabled data versus 6 days at baseline. Mean: 2.6 days with mobile-enabled data versus 27 days at baseline. Source: SSEE 2014; data link printed below the chart.
limitations: Values are read from the labels printed at the ends of the bars; no additional uncertainty or sample-size information is shown.

label: Map 2.1 — Reducing poverty: Mapping pockets of poverty in Croatia allowed better targeting of antipoverty funds
summary: Choropleth map of Croatian municipalities showing the percentage of the population living in poverty, with municipal boundaries and Zagreb marked as the national capital.
details: Croatia is subdivided into colored municipal areas. Legend, “% of population living in poverty”: 1–12 (dark green), 13–21 (green), 22–31 (yellow), 32–42 (orange), and 43–71 (red). A black star marks the national capital, Zagreb; boundary symbols distinguish international boundaries from municipality boundaries. Neighboring places labeled include Slovenia, Hungary, Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro, and Italy. Source: World Bank 2016a. Data at http://bit.do/WDR2021-Map-2_1. Map imprint: IBRD CRO45401 | MARCH 2021.
limitations: The map shows categorized municipal percentages; exact values for individual municipalities are not printed or legible. Colors and boundaries are visible, but the image does not provide a municipality name key.

label: Map 2.2
summary: Map of Bogotá showing citizen-collected safety ratings around bike paths, with most mapped points appearing in the excellent category and a pie chart reporting 81%, 15%, 3%, and 1%.
details: Title: “Improving public safety: The use of citizen-collected data in Bogotá led to greater safety around bike paths.” The map depicts Bogotá and its urban perimeter, with surrounding place labels including Funza, Mosquera, and Soacha. Legend “Safety ratings, bike paths” lists Excellent (dark teal), Very good (green), Good (yellow), Fair (light orange), Poor (red), and Bogotá urban perimeter. Colored safety-rating points are densely distributed through the urban area; dark-teal points are visually most prevalent, with other categories interspersed. An inset pie chart shows 81%, 15%, 3%, and 1%; the labels are visible but the corresponding category-to-slice mapping is not fully clear. Source: Safetipin 2016. Note: “Safety ratings of poor to excellent for Bogotá bike paths are based on safety scores.”
limitations: The map is a detailed, low-resolution reproduction; exact point counts and precise geographic boundaries cannot be read. Pie-chart category labels are not visibly linked unambiguously to every percentage.

label: Figure 2.3 — Gaps in geospatial datasets are especially large in lower-income countries
summary: Grouped bar chart comparing the share of countries with gaps in three geospatial datasets across four income groups. Lower-income countries show the largest gaps in each dataset.
details: Vertical axis: “Share of countries with dataset gaps (%)”, from 0 to 100 with gridlines at 20-point intervals. Horizontal axis: “Datasets”; categories are Administrative boundaries, Addresses and locations, and National maps. Legend: Low-income (purple), Lower-middle-income (orange), Upper-middle-income (green), High-income (blue). Bar heights, read approximately from the plotted grid: Administrative boundaries—80%, 55%, 50%, 29%, respectively; Addresses and locations—100%, 89%, 90%, 61%; National maps—100%, 61%, 40%, 24%. Values are not printed on bars, so these are visual estimates. Source printed below: WDR 2021 team calculations, based on Open Knowledge Foundation, GODI (Global Open Data Index) database; URL and data link are printed.
limitations: Bar values are not labeled numerically; values above are approximate readings from the chart.

label: Figure B2.3.1 — Proportion of COVID-19 cases reported with sex-disaggregated data for 190 countries
summary: Stacked monthly bars show the share of countries reporting COVID-19 cases with sex-disaggregated data (Yes) versus without it (No), March–November 2020; an orange line shows the proportion of countries reporting sex-disaggregated data.
details: Vertical axis is Percent, 0–100, with ticks at 0, 25, 50, 75, and 100. Horizontal axis lists March through November; “2020” is printed beneath. Each stacked bar totals 100%; green denotes “Yes” and blue denotes “No.” Approximate green shares by month, read from the bars: March 61%, April 25%, May 69%, June 30%, July 40%, August 72%, September 74%, October 60%, November 60%. The orange line, labeled “Proportion of countries reporting sex-disaggregated data,” rises from about 13% in March to about 49% in July, then stays around 45–47% through November. The figure title specifies 190 countries. Source note cites Global Health 50/50 and University College London’s COVID-19 Sex-Disaggregated Data Tracker (November 30, 2020 release), Our World in Data, and Open Data Watch calculations.
limitations: Bar and line values are estimated from the plotted marks; exact monthly values are not printed. The source note includes database links.

label: Figure 2.4
summary: Stacked bar chart compares poverty-data comparability across income groups, regions, and FCS status; lower-income and FCS economies have a larger share with noncomparable or fewer than three poverty data points.
details: Vertical 100% stacked bars; y-axis is “Share of countries (%)” with ticks 0, 20, 40, 60, 80, 100. label: Figure 2.11 — Policies to realize the potential of public intent data
summary: Policy framework linking four barriers—financing, technical capacity, governance, and data demand—to actions for national statistical offices (NSOs), other government agencies, and civil society and academia. A political-commitment banner spans all four areas.
details:
The diagram is organized as four columns (Financing; Technical capacity; Governance; Data demand) and three actor rows (NSOs; Other government agencies; Civil society and academia). Across the top, a green banner states: “Political commitment — Create a broad-based political and societal agreement on the value of high-quality public intent data.”

Financing:
• NSOs: Create a target fraction of government spending or a line item in the national budget dedicated to the NSO; engage recurrently with the Ministry of Finance to understand and support its data needs.
• Other government agencies: Designate a budget line for data in each ministry and agency; ensure use of produced data across the public sector for monitoring, evaluation, and more.
• Civil society and academia: Allocate resources to citizen-generated data collection.

Technical capacity:
• NSOs: Ensure more competitive pay scales; devote more time and resources to building capacity among staff.
• Other government agencies: Create technical units in charge of data production and use; create a governmentwide approach to the salaries of statisticians and data scientists.
• Civil society and academia: Promote data literacy in primary and secondary education; enhance tertiary education in data science and statistics.

Governance:
• NSOs: Ensure that NSO independence is anchored in laws and institutional setup; prevent statistical laws from becoming outdated.
• Other government agencies: Assign clear roles, mandates, and responsibilities along the data life cycle for government agencies (see chapters 8 and 9).
• Civil society and academia: Ensure that laws and regulations facilitate the safe dissemination of data.

Data demand:
• NSOs: Build trust in integrity of official statistics via public release calendars and best practices in dissemination; engage proactively with nongovernmental entities.
• Other government agencies: Designate knowledge brokers in government agencies to champion the flow and use of data; institutionalize data-intensive management practices.
• Civil society and academia: Enable citizens to engage more easily with data through open data platforms, machine readability, and data visualizations.

The colored actor-row labels are purple for NSOs, blue for other government agencies, and orange for civil society and academia. Source: WDR 2021 team. Note: The figure summarizes policies governments can enact, categorized by the actors and barriers they primarily address. Many policies span several actors and barriers but are placed into one box here for simplification. The role of the private sector is discussed in chapter 4; the role of international organizations is examined in spotlight 2.2. NSO = national statistical office.
limitations: The figure’s note says policies may span several actors and barriers, but are placed in one box for simplification. No quantitative data or scales are shown.

label: Table 4.1 — Selected research gaps to be addressed to advance the use of private intent data for development
summary: Two-column table listing seven research areas and example research questions about advancing the use of private intent data for development. Alternating pale-green row shading; no numeric data.
details:
Columns: “Research area” and “Examples of research gaps.” Rows and visible questions:
• Societal impacts — ensuring algorithmic policy making leads to fair outcomes; increasing transparency and interpretability of policy predictions using private intent data; safeguarding algorithms against manipulation; trade-offs between granularity and precision and the optimal mix for targeting development programs.
• Quality standards — how standards can be created, agreed on, updated, and communicated to the development community, and who should participate; standards for accuracy and precision in frontier applications using private intent data or combining public and private intent data so policy makers can trust and use results.
• External validityᵃ — promise of building models in data-rich countries and applying them in data-limited countries; avoiding data profiling and discrimination when using pre-trained models from higher-income countries for novel development uses; extent to which applications combining public intent survey data and private intent data can predict values calculated from within-country census data.
• Machine learning — how machine-learning approaches and spatial feature selection should change for specialized development-policy tasks; which features best predict spatial variation in development outcomes across contexts and the trade-offs between predictive accuracy and cost.
• Training and validation data — required volume and approach for collecting public intent data to calibrate and validate machine-learning algorithms combining public and private intent data.
• Deidentificationᵇ — how methods should change to protect individuals and companies when private intent data are used for public benefit; effects of spatial deidentification of public intent data on accuracy and precision of applications using it to calibrate and validate algorithms that combine public and private intent data.
• Capturing longitudinal change — differences in accuracy and precision between estimating longitudinal change and cross-sectional predictions of the same outcome; features that best predict longitudinal change; ensuring stability over time of algorithms predicting policy-outcome changes; effects of satellite imagery spatial, spectral, and temporal resolution on prediction accuracy and precision when survey data are combined with imagery-derived spatial features; whether effects vary with satellite imagery grid size used to extract features.
Footnotes: ᵃ External validity means findings from one location holding true in another. ᵇ “Deidentification” is used instead of anonymization because data may become identifiable as computing and machine learning advance, so may never be truly anonymized. ᶜ “Spectral” refers to different wavelengths; satellite images typically have multiple bands capturing different spectral ranges.
limitations: The table contains research questions rather than measured results; it provides no numerical values or units. Superscript footnote markers are reproduced as shown.

label: Table 5.1 — Recommendations for data infrastructure improvements sequenced according to a maturity model

Columns: Stage of country | Connecting people | Connecting countries.

label: Table 6.2 — Recommendations organized according to a maturity model based on data safeguards and enablers
summary: Three-stage maturity model table comparing recommended safeguards and enablers for a country’s data system: establishing fundamentals, initiating data flows, and optimizing the system.
details:
The table has three columns: “Stage of country’s data system,” “Safeguards,” and “Enablers.” Rows and content:

• Establishing fundamentals. Safeguards: Conduct a baseline needs assessment. Develop a comprehensive policy framework based on best practices that (1) safeguards personal, nonpersonal, and evolving categories of data and promotes greater equity around data; (2) enhances the security of systems and infrastructure that protect against misuse of data; (3) expands individuals’ agency and control over their personal data; and (4) promotes certainty and predictability, integrating fundamental safeguards discussed in the chapter, such as data protection and cybersecurity. Enablers: Conduct a baseline needs assessment. Develop a comprehensive policy framework based on best practices that enables the use and sharing of data for development purposes, ensuring access, openness, interoperability, portability, predictability, and transparency, while integrating fundamental enablers discussed in the chapter, such as electronic transactions.

• Initiating data flows. Safeguards: Elaborate a legal framework embodying policy prerogatives that include personal data protection; promotion of cybersecurity and combating cybercrime; regulation of competition; and provisions for establishing relevant enforcement institutions. Enablers: Elaborate a legal framework embodying policy prerogatives that include legal recognition of e-transactions; access to information; intellectual property rights for nonpersonal data; openness of public intent data, including use of licenses that encourage data sharing; and data classification principles.

• Optimizing the system. Safeguards: Promote awareness of safeguards domestically through adoption of data protection by design and default, together with associated cybersecurity measures; internationally through cross-border interoperability of data protection standards; address more complex issues such as mixed data and group rights; ensure sufficient capacity of institutions responsible for oversight; and establish metrics to monitor and evaluate implementation and enforcement of these policies and laws. Enablers: Consider issues such as data portability and increasing incentives around sharing private intent data; ensure sufficient capacity of institutions responsible for oversight; and establish metrics to monitor and evaluate implementation of these policies, laws, and institutions.

Source: WDR 2021 team. No numeric units or values; the table is qualitative.
limitations: Text and table structure are legible. No material ambiguity detected.

label: Figure 7.5 — Three distinct approaches to handling cross-border data flows
summary: Infographic compares limited, conditional, and open transfers models by regulatory options, key features, and examples, arranged along a data-closure to data-openness spectrum.
details:
The figure is organized into three model groups, with vertical row labels at left: “Regulatory options,” “Key features,” and “Examples.” Left-to-right, from greater data closure toward greater data openness:

• Limited transfers model (blue), divided into three regulatory-option columns:
  – Domestic storage. Key feature: broad requirements to use domestic servers for data storage. Examples: China—certain personal data; US states—government data; Australia and United Kingdom—health data; Russian Federation—telecommunications data.
  – Domestic processing. Key feature: broad requirements to use domestic servers for data processing. Example: Russian Federation—processing of personal data.
  – Government approval. Key feature: prior approval required for data transfers. Example: China—Cybersecurity Law.
• Conditional transfers model (green), regulatory option “Regulatory safeguards.” Key features: consent; adequacy findings; private sector assessment (for example, codes of conduct, binding corporate rules, contractual arrangements). Example: European Union—General Data Protection Regulation.
• Open transfers model (orange), regulatory option “Private standards.” Key features: no a priori mandatory requirements; private sector accountability based on voluntary standards. Examples: US federal rules; APEC Privacy Framework.

A horizontal gradient arrow beneath the groups runs from “Data closure” on the left to “Data openness” on the right. Source: WDR 2021 team, based on Casalini and López González (2019); Cory (2017). Note: APEC = Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation.
limitations: The graphic is a categorical comparison, not a quantitative chart; it gives no numerical scale or measured values. The source note expands APEC.

label: Table 8.1 — Data management decisions along the data life cycle
summary: Two-column table lists seven data life-cycle stages and management decisions for each, including consent, standardization, security, sharing, analysis, archiving, and destruction or reuse.
details: Columns: “Stage of life cycle” and “Area in which data management is needed.” Rows: Create/receive — Determine lawful use (such as obtaining consent for data collection and sharing); collect identifications that allow data to be merged with other datasets. Process — Standardize units and categories (such as industry classifications); use data formats that are widely compatible and accessible; validate the quality (accuracy), relevance, and integrity of data. Store — Encrypt data; use secure servers; back up and archive data. Transfer/share — Verify whether consent allows for data to be shared; deidentify data, if appropriate (footnote a); sign confidentiality agreements for use of identified data; publish data via bulk downloads or APIs. Analyze and use — Ensure reproducibility; publish code or algorithms; do not publish identifiable data; visualize and communicate insights from data. Archive and preserve — Classify and catalog data systematically so they can be found easily; include data dictionaries and notes on how data were created; maintain access to data and their security and integrity over time. Destroy or reuse — Keep records of destruction processes; verify that consent for use is still valid. Source: WDR 2021 team. Note: APIs = application programming interfaces. Footnote a: See Elliot et al. (2016); Polonetsky, Tene, and Finch (2016).
limitations: No apparent unreadable values.

label: Table 8.2 — Candidate institutions and actors to perform or inform data governance functions
summary: Four thematic clusters pair data-governance functions with indicative institutions and actors: strategic planning, rule making and implementation, compliance, and learning and evidence.
details: Two columns: “Thematic clusters and functions” and “Indicative institutions and actors.” Strategic planning: developing strategies and policies in line with the social contract for data; establishing institutional arrangements. Indicative actors: data governance arrangement (centralized agency/unit embedded in an existing institution, such as NSO or digital economy ministry; or decentralized units and responsibilities embedded across government), CSOs, universities, research institutions. Learning and evidence: engaging in backward-looking monitoring and evaluation; engaging in forward-looking learning and risk management. Actors under “Knowledge community”: M&E unit within entity or independent M&E body; CSOs and NGOs, multilateral development institutions, international development banks; academic institutions; think tanks, policy institutes, research institutions; news media; training bodies; professional associations. Source: WDR 2021 team, based on a functional approach to governance and public sector management. Note expands CSIRT, CSO, IMF, M&E, NGO, NSO, SSO, UN, and WTO.

label: Table 8.3 — Snapshot of common data intermediary structures
summary: Four-column table comparing purposes, objectives, intermediary types, and examples across commercial data markets, collaborative data sharing, and trusted sharing of sensitive data.
details: Columns: Purposes | Objectives | Types | Examples. Rows (some purpose cells span multiple rows): 1) Create commercial value and data markets. | Transform raw data into more consumable information. | Data aggregators, data brokers | Acxiom, Experian. 2) Exchange data to solve public problems through collaborative structures. | Increase incentives for competitors to share and combine data resources for common use within sectors. | Data pools | Global Data Synchronization Network (GDSN). 3) Same purpose as row 2. | Create and manage shared and interoperable data assets and computing infrastructure for research. | Data commons, data clubs | The Open Commons Consortium (OCC), UK Biobank. 4) Same purpose as row 2. | Contribute data in exchange for collective benefits. | Data cooperatives | LunaDNA (community-owned platform for health research). 5) Enable trusted sharing and use of sensitive data through enhanced accountability mechanisms. | Facilitate sharing of sensitive data and provide collective bargaining power to individuals. | Data trusts | Platform Info Exchange, UK (Mozilla Data Futures Lab pilot). limitations: No numeric values. The purpose in row 2 spans the data pools, data commons/data clubs, and data cooperatives entries; the table’s merged-cell layout is reflected in the details.

label: Figure 8.7 — Features of well-functioning institutions for effective data governance
summary: Six interlocking puzzle pieces identify institutional features for effective data governance, grouped under a performance-enhancing environment.
details: The diagram is a connected, six-piece puzzle. At left, a bracket-like outline labels the overall environment “Performance-enhancing environment.” The top row contains: (1) Coordination — “Create incentives to encourage collaborative and user-centric decision-making.” (2) Leadership — “Mobilize data champions in positions of power to create a culture of data sharing and use.” (3) Multistakeholder governance — “Sustain outcomes through inclusive and legitimate stakeholder engagement.” The bottom row contains: (4) Transparency — “Build trust by promoting participation and accountability in policy making.” (5) Functional autonomy — “Promote institutional independence and autonomy for effective performance.” (6) Data literacy — “Invest in increasing technical capacity, resources, and data skills for civil servants.” Source printed below: “WDR 2021 team.”
limitations: No quantitative scale or values are shown; the puzzle-piece layout conveys a set of connected features, not a specified sequence or ranking.

label: Figure 9.1 — What happens in an integrated national data system?
summary: Four stacked, color-outlined bands describe what happens to data, who participates, the pillars of the system, and the foundation that sustains it.
details: Top-to-bottom structure: “Data are” produced, protected, open, quality controlled, and used and reused. “By” government entities; civil society and individuals; academic institutions; the private sector; international organizations. “Built on the pillars of” infrastructure policies; laws and regulations; economic policies; institutions. “Sustained by the foundation of” human capital; trust; funding; incentives; data demand. Each item is accompanied by an icon. Source: WDR 2021 team.
limitations: The diagram shows grouped components, not explicit directional arrows or quantitative values.

label: Figure 9.2 — A data maturity model for a hypothetical national data system
summary: Circular maturity model shows three concentric stages across five participant groups; darker segment colors indicate steps accomplished and lighter colors steps not accomplished.
details: A segmented circular diagram has three maturity rings, labeled from the center outward: “Establishing fundamentals” (orange), “Initiating data flows” (green), and “Optimizing the system” (blue). The outer dark-purple ring identifies five participant groups around the circle: Government entities; Civil society and individuals; Academic institutions; Private sector; International organizations. Each participant’s three ring segments are independently shaded dark or light, illustrating differing progress among participants and stages. Callout labels at the upper-left of the rings point to the three stages. Source: WDR 2021 team.
limitations: The diagram is illustrative and has no numeric scale or values. Segment shading is visible, but the note does not specify a quantitative measure of completion.

label: Figure 9.3 — Steps to integrating the public sector into the national data system
summary: Three overlapping, progressively positioned panels describe steps for integrating the public sector into the national data system: establishing fundamentals, initiating data flows, and optimizing the system.
details: The diagram has three overlapping rounded panels arranged from left/back to right/front. Orange panel, “Establishing fundamentals”: Policies—recognize the importance of an integrated national data system in a high-level strategic document; Laws and regulations—put in place robust data protection regulations; Human capital and funding—strengthen the technical capacity and financing of NSOs; Institutions—create technical units in ministries to strengthen administrative data and coordinate data efforts across ministries; Incentives—ensure public-sector data scientists and statisticians are appropriately remunerated. Green panel, “Initiating data flows”: Data demand—establish a culture of data use in ministries and among policy makers and legislators; Incentives—prioritize open data for development and use of common standards throughout the data life cycle; Infrastructure policies—establish a secure, integrated digital platform for storing and providing access to deidentified public intent data. Blue panel, “Optimizing the system”: Institutions—charge an existing or new government unit with responsibility for overseeing and reporting on implementation of a national data strategy; Incentives—empower the NSO to take an active role in the national data system; Policies—define clear institutional mandates for the various government institutions. Source: WDR 2021 team. Note: Categories overlap and are meant to be illustrative. NSO = national statistical office.
limitations: The panels overlap; the note explicitly says categories overlap and are illustrative. No arrows or explicit causal links are shown.

label: Figure 9.4 — Steps to integrating civil society into the national data system
summary: Three overlapping, progressively layered panels outline steps for integrating civil society into the national data system: establishing fundamentals, initiating data flows, and optimizing the system.
details: Left orange panel, “Establishing fundamentals”: • Laws and regulations: Institute laws protecting people’s rights to produce, use, and disseminate data. • Incentives: Create civil society watchdogs to monitor compliance with the rules of the system. • Funding: Ensure that civil society has sufficient funding and resources for data production and use. Middle green panel, “Initiating data flows”: • Human capital: Improve data literacy through joint projects, training, and secondments and through the education system. • Infrastructure policies: Ensure adoption of common standards that improve data quality and interoperability. • Trust: Promote trust through establishment of an independent scientific quality control unit. Right blue panel, “Optimizing the system”: • Institutions: Institutionalize collaboration for the systematic use of citizen-generated data in decision-making. • Incentives: Include civil society in planning, high-level decisions, and strategy setting for the national data system. Panels overlap visually; note says categories overlap and are meant to be illustrative. Source: WDR 2021 team.
limitations: No quantitative values or axes. Text is legible; panel overlap is intentional and does not specify a strict sequence.

label: Figure 9.5 — Steps to integrating academia into the national data system
summary: Three overlapping, progressively layered panels list actions for integrating academia into the national data system: establishing fundamentals, initiating data flows, and optimizing the system.
details: The diagram has three overlapping rounded panels, arranged from largest/rearmost to smaller/frontmost. Establishing fundamentals (orange, left/rear): Infrastructure policies—ensure academics have adequate financial support and access to key ICT infrastructure; Data demand—promote awareness of participants’ datasets by building relationships among partners in academia and government. Initiating data flows (green, center): Data demand—set up data-sharing agreements, commission data production by academics, and support repurposing of academic data; Human capital—promote data literacy through quantitative degree programs, workshops, and secondments. Optimizing the system (blue, right/front): Infrastructure policies—institutionalize access to data through data portals and data enclaves; Data demand—support and adopt data innovations by academia; Incentives—support initiatives that provide legal access to scientific journals. Source: WDR 2021 team. Note: Categories overlap and are meant to be illustrative. ICT = information and communication technology.
limitations: The diagram explicitly says categories overlap and are illustrative; the panel overlap indicates stages but does not specify a strict sequence or directional arrows.

label: Figure 9.6 — Steps to integrating the private sector into the national data system
summary: Three overlapping, progressively layered panels outline steps for establishing fundamentals, initiating data flows, and optimizing the national data system for private-sector participation.
details: The diagram uses three overlapping rounded panels. Left/orange panel, “Establishing fundamentals”: (1) Infrastructure policies — construct national transmission networks for high-speed wireless broadband access; (2) Human capital — equip workers and businesses with the skills and appliances needed to produce and use data. Center/green panel, “Initiating data flows”: (1) Infrastructure policies — increase IXPs and data centers to improve the efficiency of data transfers; (2) Incentives — adopt compensation and noncompensation schemes to promote data exchanges; (3) Data demand — promote the role of data stewards in business. Right/blue panel, “Optimizing the system”: (1) Incentives — increase data interoperability through adoption of stringent data quality and privacy standards that are also pro-business; (2) Infrastructure policies — promote expansion of and access to colocation data centers; (3) Trust — engage business through trusted data intermediaries. Source: WDR 2021 team. Note: Categories overlap and are meant to be illustrative. IXPs = internet exchange points. The panels overlap visually; they present categories/steps, not an explicit directional flow or quantitative scale.
limitations: No quantitative values, axes, or explicit arrows are shown.

label: Figure 9.7 — Steps to integrating international and regional organizations into the national data system and collaborating across borders
summary: Three overlapping, progressively positioned panels list ways to integrate international and regional organizations into national data systems: establishing fundamentals, initiating data flows, and optimizing the system.
details:
The diagram has three overlapping rounded panels, arranged from a large orange panel at left/back to a green panel in the middle and a blue panel at right/front. No arrows are shown; the panel placement suggests successive stages, while the note says categories overlap and are illustrative.

• Establishing fundamentals (orange): Funding — “Seek the support needed, including technical assistance, to improve weak parts of the data life cycle.” Human capital — “Increase technical capacity and data literacy.” Institutions — “Engage in regional data cooperation to save resources through economies of scale and facilitate peer-to-peer learning.”
• Initiating data flows (green): Data demand — “Introduce definitions and standards into national data systems that are comparable across countries.” Infrastructure policies — “Adopt common standards to enable cross-border data flows.”
• Optimizing the system (blue): Incentives — “Coordinate and align data production and information sharing across international organizations active domestically.” Institutions — “Help shape the priorities of the data agendas of international organizations.” Economic policies — “Participate in negotiation of trade agreements on data and in international and regional tax treaties.”
Source: WDR 2021 team. Note: Categories overlap and are meant to be illustrative.
limitations: The diagram presents illustrative categories, not a quantified sequence or measured outcomes. The panels overlap, and their ordering does not establish that every country follows the same progression.
